Whether you're discovering your next favorite band or just vibing with the mood, this Vale
f: Love is in the air on the farm 💓 This week’s PICK26 artists lean into soul, harmony, and swoon, bringing together lowrider soul, lush vocals, and dream-like soundscapes made for falling in love with new music. Whether you’re discovering your next favorite band or just vibing with the mood, this Valentine’s drop is all heart.
Early bird tickets are on sale now! Grab yours while they last and save on the lowest priced tickets of the year.

You can’t fake this pedigree. As the granddaughters of Sam Cooke and daughters of Cecil and Linda Womack, these three sisters literally have the history of American Soul music in their blood. But they aren’t a nostalgia act; they bring a modern, polished R&B swagger to that legacy. It’s timeless without feeling dusty.

We believe in blood harmony. There is a specific resonance that only happens when siblings sing together, and The Womack Sisters have it mastered. We picked them because they represent the continuum of Soul—honoring the past while singing clearly to the future.

Lead by Joey Quinones, Thee Sinseers are the leaders of the East L.A. “Souldies” movement. This is music that drives slow and hurts good. It’s a revival of that sweet, romantic soul music of the mid-century, complete with brass sections, matching suits, and falsetto vocals that will make the toughest person in the crowd swoon.

We are suckers for a love song. In a festival environment that can be high-energy and frantic, Thee Sinseers provide a moment of collective romance. We booked them because this music transcends generations—it hits the nostalgia button for the old heads, but it feels fresh and vital for the younger crowd.
The Vibe: Radical Honesty in Three-Part Harmony

Don’t let the name fool you (or maybe do)—this Australian trio is raw, funny, and devastatingly intimate. They channel the energy of Boygenius or CSnY, stripping the music down to just voices and guitars so you have no choice but to listen to the lyrics. It’s confessional songwriting that feels like reading a diary entry out loud.

We love the quiet moments that stop the festival dead in its tracks. We booked Folk Bitch Trio because they have the power to hush a crowd of thousands. This is going to be one of those “you could hear a pin drop” sets under the trees.
The Vibe: A Lynchian Western Dream

Molly Hamilton and Robert Earl Thomas make music that sounds like a cowboy movie directed by a shoegaze band. It’s breathy, atmospheric, and full of “cowboy chords” that float in the air like smoke. This is music for drifting—perfectly suited for a late afternoon where the light is hitting the trees just right.

Pickathon has always loved the intersection of “Roots” and “Atmosphere.” Widowspeak captures that specific Pacific Northwest mood—slightly melancholic, incredibly beautiful, and deeply textured. We booked them to be the soundtrack for your most cinematic moment in the woods.

stories.t: PICK26: Marcos Valle, Built to Spill & New Sounds
stories.x: From Rio de Janeiro to Boise. Discover why Marcos Valle, Built to Spill, The Brothers Comatose and Automatic are essential viewing at Pickathon 2026.
stories.b: From Rio's golden-hour grooves to the roots of Northwest indie rock, this round of PICK26 brings together Marcos Valle, Built to Spill, The Brothers Comatose, and Automatic for a full-spectrum journey across continents, decades, and genres. Discover why these artists are essential viewing at Pickath
f: From Rio’s golden-hour grooves to the roots of Northwest indie rock, this round of PICK26 brings together Marcos Valle, Built to Spill, The Brothers Comatose, and Automatic for a full-spectrum journey across continents, decades, and genres. Discover why these artists are essential viewing at Pickathon 2026, then dive into the official playlist below.
The Vibe: Rio de Janeiro Golden Hour

If you think Bossa Nova is just quiet background music, Marcos Valle is here to correct the record. He is a titan of Brazilian music—a man who sat at the table with the founders of the genre in the 60s, but then spent the next five decades injecting it with funk, disco, and psychedelic rock. He represents the resilient spirit of Rio, surviving dictatorships and changing trends by simply refusing to stop grooving.

We wanted a legend who could control the sun. There is a specific type of magic that happens when a master like Valle takes the stage; the air gets lighter. It’s rare to book an artist who is historically significant enough to be in a museum, but whose music still makes you want to dance with a stranger.
The Vibe: The DNA of Northwest Indie Rock

Before Modest Mouse, before Death Cab for Cutie, there was Doug Martsch and Built to Spill. They are the architects of the specific guitar-heavy, sprawling, emotional indie rock sound that put the Pacific Northwest on the map. Doug’s guitar playing doesn’t show off; it tells stories, looping, intricate, and instantly recognizable.

This is a homecoming. Built to Spill’s music was practically made to be heard under a canopy of fir trees. We booked them because their songs have a “stamina” to them, extended jams and guitar textures that reward you for closing your eyes and just listening. It’s a nod to the roots of the indie scene that Pickathon grew out of.
The Vibe: The Rowdiest Living Room on Earth

Some bluegrass bands are for sitting and studying; The Brothers Comatose are for standing on the furniture. They play with the loose, sweaty energy of a garage rock band, but swap the electric guitars for a banjo and upright bass. It’s unpretentious, high-octane Americana that feels like a party you stumbled into by accident and stayed at until 3 AM.

We need ignition. A festival needs bands that can turn a tired crowd into a dancing mob in under 60 seconds, and The Brothers Comatose are the best in the business. We booked them for the sheer joy of it—because sometimes you just need to stomp your boots.

Automatic strips rock and roll down to the studs. A trio of bass, drums, and synths (no guitars allowed), they play motorik, Krautrock-inspired post-punk that is deadpan, hypnotic, and incredibly tight. It’s music that feels mechanical yet deeply human, driving forward with a relentless rhythm.

We book the leaders of the genre. Automatic is currently defining the sound of the modern underground by rejecting the excess of rock music. We picked them because they represent a sharp, intelligent counterpoint to the organic sounds of the farm. They prove you don’t need six strings to be heavy; you just need the right groove.

stories.x: We’re proud to celebrate 12 Pickathon alumni who are nominated across 23 Grammy nominations in 17 categories, spanning roots, country, bluegrass, jazz, alternative, and beyond.

f: For more than two decades, Pickathon has trusted its instincts, booking artists not for where they already are, but for where they’re headed. Every year, musicians step onto stages built in the woods, surrounded by trees, community, and curiosity. The setting is humble. The intention is not.
This year, that long view feels especially affirmed.

We’re proud to celebrate 12 Pickathon alumni who are nominated across 23 Grammy nominations in 17 categories, spanning roots, country, bluegrass, jazz, alternative, and beyond. These nominations honor artists who once played on the farm and are now being recognized on one of music’s biggest stages.

Pickathon has never been about predicting awards. It’s about creating space for artists to take risks, for audiences to discover something new, and for music to exist in a way that feels human, communal, and alive. The farm doesn’t manufacture moments; it makes room for them.
Below is the full list of Grammy nominations represented by Pickathon alumni this year.

Seeing these artists recognized across so many categories is a reminder that when music is given the right conditions… time, trust, and a listening audience… it grows.
To all of the artists who have shared their songs in the woods: congratulations.We’re grateful you passed through the forest — and we can’t wait to hear what comes next.
The 68th Grammy Awards will air on February 1, 2026.

stories.t: PICK26: Steve Earle, Shakey Graves, and more, shaping the sound of Pickathon
stories.x: The legends who built the road and the artists driving it now.
stories.b: For 26 years, Pickathon has built its lineup through instinct, intention, and trust in the long view of music. PICK26 is our artist spotlight series—an inside look at why Pickathon picked these artists for the 2026 lineup. These first spotlights set the tone, honoring the architects who shaped the s
f: For 26 years, Pickathon has built its lineup through instinct, intention, and trust in the long view of music. PICK26 is our artist spotlight series—an inside look at why Pickathon picked these artists for the 2026 lineup. These first spotlights set the tone, honoring the architects who shaped the sounds we love while highlighting a few of the voices carrying them forward.

Steve Earle is the bridge between the outlaw country of Townes Van Zandt and the modern Americana world. He has lived nine lives—from “Copperhead Road” to the depths of addiction and back again—and he sings with the grit of a survivor. He isn’t just a musician; he is a historian of the American experience.

We picked Steve because you need a North Star. In a lineup full of new sounds, he grounds the festival in the absolute truth of songwriting. Watching him play in the woods is a bucket-list moment—a master class in how three chords and the truth can still stop the world.
The Vibe: The Prodigal Son Returns.

Alejandro Rose-Garcia (Shakey Graves) started as a one-man band with a suitcase drum and has evolved into a genre-bending rock star. He is the ultimate Pickathon success story—a chaotic, charismatic performer who can shift from a whisper to a scream in a single measure.

We love a homecoming. Shakey is part of the farm’s DNA. We brought him back as a headliner not for nostalgia, but because he is playing the best music of his life right now. He embodies the “Pickathon Spirit”—wild, unpredictable, and impossible to categorize.

Coming straight out of Southeast L.A., The Altons are the soundtrack to a late-night cruise with the windows down. They blend classic soul with a touch of rocksteady and Latin rhythm. Bryan Ponce’s vocals have that rare, rasping quality that feels like it’s coming from a vintage jukebox.
We booked The Altons for the “Swoon Factor.” In a lineup full of high-energy shredding, they provide the groove. This is music for holding hands and swaying.

This isn’t pop-country; this is the real deal. Hannah Juanita plays honky-tonk music for the heartbreak crowd, channeling the spirit of Loretta Lynn and Patsy Cline. It’s steel guitars, crying fiddles, and stories about loving the wrong people.

We booked her for the purists. Every year, we look for that one voice that can transport you straight to a 1970s Nashville dive bar, and Hannah is it. She cuts through the noise with pure, unadulterated storytelling.

stories.t: The 2026 Lineup: Where Legends Play the Woods and The Future is Born
stories.x: After 26 years of elevating emerging artists like Geese, Billy Strings and Leon Bridges, the Portland-area festival returns with a lineup that balances discovery with icons including Steve Earle, Shakey Graves and Marcos Valle.

Pickathon returns to Pendarvis Farm July 30–Aug
f: After 26 years of elevating emerging artists like Geese, Billy Strings and Leon Bridges, the Portland-area festival returns with a lineup that balances discovery with icons including Steve Earle, Shakey Graves, Marcos Valle, and The Travelin’ McCourys.

Pickathon returns to Pendarvis Farm July 30–August 2, 2026, continuing its tradition as the country’s most distinct music festival experience. For its 26th year, the festival presents a unique curation strategy: We are honoring the pioneers who built the genres we love while handing the main stages over to the vanguard artists who are reinventing them.
Championing the widest sonic range in the country, the 2026 bill is anchored by the “Legends,” a tier celebrating musical architects with deep legacies including master songwriter Steve Earle.

The history of sound is represented across every border: from the bossa nova royalty of Marcos Valle and the Jamaican roots reggae of Clinton Fearon to the psychedelic cumbia of Bogotá’s Meridian Brothers. We celebrate the pioneers of heavy sound with doom metal legends Acid King and the electronic-folk fusion of Mexican Institute of Sound, alongside indie rock heroes Built to Spill and the folk troubadour herself, Alela Diane. Finally, Pickathon welcomes back its own prodigal son, Shakey Graves, returning as a festival headliner and a modern classic in his own right.
A Track Record You Can Trust

While the legends set the tone, the true headline is discovery. For 26 years, Pickathon has served as the industry’s crystal ball—the stage where fans first encountered The War on Drugs, Kamasi Washington, Tyler Childers, The Marías, Black Pumas, Khruangbin and Big Thief, long before they sold out arenas.
In 2026, the audience returns not just for the names they know, but to find the standout bands Pickathon puts on their radar first.
The Discovery: Titans of the Underground

This year’s roster is designed to be explored like a treasure map. As titans of their specific undergrounds—whether it’s a regional phenomenon or a niche subculture—these acts are the leading indicators of what is next in music.

Leading the charge are the “Discovery Artists”—acts currently electrifying major rooms, including the soul-revival giants The Altons and Thee Sinseers, the rowdy bluegrass titans The Brothers Comatose and indie-rock stalwarts Widowspeak.

Beyond the anchors, the festival places its bets on the wide spectrum of the future. Buzz is building around the vocal soul dynasty The Womack Sisters and the raw, glitch-heavy alternative of mercury, while the lineup shifts gears from the classic country storytelling of Hannah Juanita to the genre-bending grooves of The South Hill Experiment. We dive deeper with the rising harmonies of Folk Bitch Trio and the post-punk cool of Automatic, rounding out the discovery with the spellbinding guitar work of Hannah Frances and the poignant, lo-fi songwriting of Hudson Freeman. This section proves that the future of music is wide, wild, and happening this summer on the farm.
Don’t recognize a name? That is the point. We designed these playlists to be your roadmap. Press play and find your new favorite band before you see them in the woods.
More Ways to Listen: 📺 Watch the Official Video Playlist 🎵 Apple Music Playlist | YouTube Music Playlist | Amazon Music Playlist

Pickathon is more than a lineup; it is a temporary city built in the woods. Every summer, Pendarvis Farm is transformed by local design teams into a “Metropolis of Imagination,” featuring massive, reusable architectural stages that define distinct neighborhoods woven into the forest.

A Restorative Vacation (No Upcharge Required) We don’t believe in a “Comfort Tax.” At Pickathon, the premium experience is the standard, allowing you to disconnect from the noise and reconnect with the wild.

A Flow Designed for Discovery: Nearly every artist performs two distinct sets—perhaps one in the high-energy Galaxy Barn and another in the big leaf maple cathedral of the Woods Stage. This structure creates a relaxed pace, supported by a rotating roster of DJs, literary readings, standup comedy, and the farm-to-table Curation Series dining experience.
Comfort by Design: We prioritize your stamina. Escape the heat in artist-designed architectural lounges and deep natural shade, available to everyone without a VIP upgrade.
Summer Camp for All: From the littlest explorers to the teenagers, our dedicated family neighborhoods offer a full “Summer Camp” experience with nature-based play, workshops, and music.
And for 2026, Pickathon’s annual emblem is the Frog—joyful, at times a little absurd, and strongest as a chorus of voices, much like the world we’re building together.
“We don’t book artists because they’re obvious. We book them because they’re pointing to what’s next.” — Zale Schoenborn, Founder

f: Every year, Pickathon welcomes a new animal into our story. It represents the energy of the moment and the world we are building together.
For 2026, we chose a creature that represents the power of the leap.

Modeled after the Pacific Tree Frog native to Oregon, this year’s symbol is a master of two worlds. Frogs belong to the land and the water equally. They remind us that we don’t have to fit into just one box; we can thrive in the connection between things.
There is something joyful, and perhaps a little absurd, about the frog.

When the world feels heavy or still, the frog doesn’t harden. It waits, it watches, and then—it leaps. It is a symbol of kinetic energy. It’s the choice to move and dance, even when the rest of the woods are quiet.

A single Pacific Tree Frog is small, but a chorus of them is undeniable. They find strength in numbers. This summer, we return to the farm to raise our own chorus, bringing people together to build something loud and beautiful.

Funding the Magic: A Benefit for Creative Neighborhoods
This party has a purpose. It is a benefit for our nonprofit partner, Creative Neighborhoods.
Creative Neighborhoods is the engine that builds the world of Pickathon. They coordinate the design teams and architecture that transform Pendarvis Farm.

For 2026, we are planning over a dozen public neighborhoods. Pickathon serves as the accelerator for the nonprofits behind these spaces, helping them exceed their fundraising goals and amplify their missions.
Your ticket funds the art of 2026.
The Art & Shade: They build the woven cathedrals and “Neighborhoods” you relax in.

The Mission (People & Partners): Your support directly funds two key pillars of our impact: Workforce Activation: We deliver high-value, hands-on pre-apprenticeship training in a high-visibility, professional environment. Partner Amplification: We amplify mission stories and impact to fuel partner fundraising and achieve elevated outcomes for the community.
Proceeds from your ticket and 10% of all food and drink at the party go directly to funding these materials. Come have a drink, play some pickleball, and help build the festival.

f: Why The Magic Exists: Turning A Moment Into A Movement
As the holiday week wraps up, we are asking you to support our nonprofit partner, Creative Neighborhoods, on GivingTuesday.

We all know the feeling of walking onto the Farm. It’s the immersion of the architecture rising from the treelines, the intricate designs that hold you in the landscape, and the sense of discovery around every corner.
That experience is the direct result of Creative Neighborhoods.
It is this nonprofit work that prevents Pickathon from becoming just another daytime festival in a big, open, dusty field. It allows us to be regenerative, not extractive.

The Problem: Producing a festival is expensive. Without community support, the “mission” aspect of the festival—the experimental architecture, the education, the zero-waste systems—is always vulnerable. When budgets are tight, these are often the first things at risk of being cut.

The Solution: Creative Neighborhoods allows us to turn the temporary moment of Pickathon into a year-round movement. We create a Regenerative Ecosystem that delivers maximum impact across three critical pillars:
Circular Design Innovation: We act as a world-class lab for sustainable architecture. Our thesis is simple: What is built for a day is designed for a decade.
Workforce Empowerment: We provide high-value, hands-on training to the next generation of builders, using the festival build as a classroom.
Permanent Legacy Assets: We ensure the materials used at the festival don’t just disappear. We capture and reuse that infrastructure to build lasting assets that serve our local community year-round.
The Goal: A circular model where culture funds the structure. This gives us the platform to innovate and scale, ensuring Pickathon is reimagined, improved, and magical every single year.

f: We’re still glowing. Our 25th year together felt like a landmark moment—a celebration of not just how far we’ve come, but of the incredible community that has grown up around this festival.

It was a shared success, and we were so proud to see our community’s unique spirit recognized on a national level, with Paste Magazine highlighting how Pickathon stands apart in a world of festival clones.

This milestone is the perfect launchpad for what’s next, and for us, that future is Creative Neighborhoods. This is our most important mission yet: a blueprint for a festival that gives back more than it takes. It’s a commitment to pioneering sustainable architecture, creating a real-world classroom for emerging talent, and pursuing the ambitious goal of upcycling festival structures to create a lasting legacy.

To build this future with intention and care, we need to hear from you. Your experience—what you loved, what you noticed, what you dreamed of—is the most crucial ingredient in our planning. f: Pickathon on Film with Kelsey Jean

For our 25th anniversary, we teamed up with local Portland photographer Kelsey Jean to capture Pickathon in a way that honors both our history and the living spirit of the festival today. Guided by a creative sense of nostalgia and permission to play, Kelsey shot with expired Polaroid and 35mm film to focus on the quiet, intimate details that tell the story of a festival weekend.

Instead of only following the stage lights, her lens lingered on the in-between moments: inside jokes scrawled on napkins, handwritten setlists, the glow of sunsets filtered through our neighborhood installations, and those hidden exchanges that vanish in the blink of an eye.

The resulting images feel timeless — as if they could have been pulled from a dusty shoebox decades ago or developed fresh this morning. They are fragments of memory and artistry colliding, stitched together into a visual scrapbook of connection, celebration, and the everyday magic of being here, together.
Explore the full gallery of expired Polaroids and 35mm shots (coming soon – developing!) from Pickathon 2025 below.

stories.t: In a World of Festival Clones, Pickathon Stands Apart
stories.x: Paste Magazine captured the magic of our 25th anniversary, showing how Pickathon defies the festival formula with creative neighborhoods, eclectic curation, and a spirit of discovery.
stories.b: This summer, Pickathon celebrated its 25th year with four unforgettable days of music, art, and community at Pendarvis Farm. While we've always known there's nothing else quite like it, it was especially meaningful to see that truth captured so vividly in Paste Magazine's recent feature: In a World
f: This summer, Pickathon celebrated its 25th year with four unforgettable days of music, art, and community at Pendarvis Farm. While we’ve always known there’s nothing else quite like it, it was especially meaningful to see that truth captured so vividly in Paste Magazine’s recent feature: In a World of Festival Clones, Pickathon Stands Apart.

Paste’s Josh Jackson spent his first-ever Pickathon wandering between the Galaxy Barn and the Woods Stage, stopping to savor blackberries along the path and marvel at the architecture of our Creative Neighborhoods. What he found is what longtime Pickathon fans already know: while many festivals lean on formula and repetition, Pickathon is constantly reinventing itself.

Stages become works of art, crafted anew each year by teams of local architects and designers. Families discover shaded forest groves, while night owls lose themselves in illuminated courtyards and barn dancefloors. Everywhere you turn, there’s something unexpected — a comedy set, a poetry reading, a pop-up chef dinner, or kids busking in the woods.

As founder Zale Schoenborn shared, Pickathon has always been about curation — not just booking the obvious headliners, but finding artists that attendees will fall in love with. That meant 2025 was filled with moments like:
Portugal. The Man, Taj Mahal, Fruit Bats, and Greensky Bluegrass anchoring the lineup.
Rising voices like Humbird, Hannah Cohen, Being Dead, and Derya Yıldırım & Grup Şimşek playing multiple sets across stages.
A moving tribute to Portland folk legend Michael Hurley, uniting festival regulars in song.
It’s this balance of legacy and discovery that makes Pickathon special: you may come for one act, but you’ll leave with a dozen new favorites.

One detail that struck Jackson most wasn’t musical at all — it was the lack of trash. Thanks to reusable plates, metal cups, volunteer-powered systems, and a commitment to reusing materials (even our stages), Pickathon continues to lead the way in sustainable festival culture.
A Quarter Century In, Still Growing Strong

Paste concluded what we’ve always believed: there’s something special happening in the woods of Oregon. A quarter-century on, Pickathon is more than a festival — it’s a community experiment in creativity, sustainability, and connection.
We’re grateful to everyone who joined us for the 25th anniversary, and to Paste for capturing the spirit of Pickathon in words and photos.

stories.t: How to Conquer Pickathon (And Still Love It in the End)!
stories.x: Portland Mercury’s Holly Hazelwood set out to see every single band at our 25th anniversary — and did it, with 74 sets across four days. Her guide shows how Pickathon pushes limits, fuels discovery, and still leaves you wanting more.
stories.b: For most of us, Pickathon is about finding a rhythm — wandering between stages, discovering new artists, and soaking up the atmosphere of Pendarvis Farm. But for Portland Mercury writer Holly Hazelwood, the challenge was much bigger: see every single band at our 25th anniversary festival. She succee
f: For most of us, Pickathon is about finding a rhythm — wandering between stages, discovering new artists, and soaking up the atmosphere of Pendarvis Farm. But for Portland Mercury writer Holly Hazelwood, the challenge was much bigger: see every single band at our 25th anniversary festival.

She succeeded, clocking in an astonishing 74 sets across nearly 60 artists. In her feature, How to Conquer Pickathon (And Still Love It in the End)!, Hazelwood shares the joys, lessons, and limits of her quest. Here’s how she broke it down:
Ask Yourself, “Why Am I Doing This?”

Seeing every band at Pickathon is no small feat — and Hazelwood admits you have to be a little bit bonkers to try. But for her, the motivation was clear: after a few “laid-back” years of missing great sets, she wanted to wring every last drop out of Pickathon’s milestone year.

If you’re going to chase every act, you have to live Pickathon fully. Hazelwood arrived early on Thursday morning, pitched her tent near Windmill Stage, and set up camp close to the action. For anyone taking on the challenge, the right campsite can be the difference between making it across the farm and missing the magic.
Accept, In Advance, That You Will Be Going Into “Rest Debt”

Over four days, Hazelwood walked 30 miles between stages, often running on just four hours of sleep. Her reminder? Pickathon is both a marathon and a sprint. If you’re trying to see it all, rest is limited — but the rewards are plenty.
Pickathon Is a Marathon AND a Sprint

Thursday may feel like a warm-up day, but Hazelwood notes it’s a key chance to front-load your schedule. By pushing hard early, you free up time later in the weekend to revisit favorites or let serendipity guide you.

Pickathon regulars know: you need a schedule, but you also need to stay flexible. Hazelwood describes abandoning Portugal. The Man for a half-hour with Ben Seretan, and trading a Woods Stage set for Jimetta Rose & the Voices of Creation. Those pivots often lead to the best discoveries.
Accept That You’re Still Missing Something

Even if you catch every band, you can’t catch everything. Hazelwood recalls missing late-night wildness at the Pumphouse and dramatic stage-climbing antics at Galaxy Barn and Cherry Hill. That’s part of the Pickathon experience — knowing the festival always holds more magic than you can possibly capture.
Ask Yourself Again: “Why Am I Doing This?”

For Hazelwood, the answer was simple: to fall in love with music. Pickathon’s curation opened the door to life-changing sets from Jimetta Rose, Ben Seretan, SML, Revival Season, and countless others she might not have discovered anywhere else.

As she writes, “Completing Pickathon is a slog, but it gives anyone willing to try a chance to shake themselves loose of genre expectations… all to better understand the incredible thing happening at Pendarvis every summer.”

lk: How to Conquer Pickathon (And Still Love It in the End)

stories.t: Portland State Architecture students design, build new zero-waste stage for 2025 Pickathon festival
stories.x: Portland State Architecture students designed and built the Cherry Hill stage at Pickathon 2025 — a zero-waste Douglas fir and burlap structure that will be reused in schools and gardens after the festival.
stories.b: One of Pickathon's most beloved traditions is the debut of a brand-new stage, dreamed up and built by the students of Portland State University's School of Architecture. For our 25th anniversary, they delivered one of their most ambitious designs yet: "The Water Serpent," the serpentine structure th
f: One of Pickathon’s most beloved traditions is the debut of a brand-new stage, dreamed up and built by the students of Portland State University’s School of Architecture. For our 25th anniversary, they delivered one of their most ambitious designs yet: “The Water Serpent,” the serpentine structure that became the 2025 Cherry Hill stage.

Crafted entirely from Douglas fir lumber and reusable materials, the installation encircled the audience with a flowing, porous perimeter that invited people to move in and out of the performance space. Slatted benches tucked beneath the structure offered shady resting spots, while more than 400 strips of burlap coffee sacks rippled overhead — billowing like the gills of a trout and glowing after dark under LED light.

“Designing and building ‘The Water Serpent’ was a chance to create something poetic and alive,” shared PSU Master of Architecture student Nati Ochoa. “When the wind catches the high burlap layers and the light filters through, the whole structure feels like it’s breathing.”

Over the weekend, the Cherry Hill neighborhood hosted more than 30 artists and DJs, including Fruit Bats, Surprise Chef, and PSU alum Haley Heynderickx, giving festival-goers an unforgettable backdrop for music discovery.
As with every PSU collaboration since 2014, the stage was built to live beyond Pickathon. After the festival:
The lumber will be repurposed in Portland Public Schools shop programs and a new classroom structure at the PSU Oak Savanna.
The burlap fabric will find new life as weed control in community gardens.
This zero-waste approach ensures each stage is not only a work of art for one magical weekend but also a contribution to the community for years to come.

Past PSU stages have been made from everything from wooden shipping pallets and giant cardboard tubes to apple bins and electric-cable reels, each finding reuse in shelters, villages, and community projects across Oregon. The program, guided by professors Clive Knights and Travis Bell, has been recognized by outlets like ArchDaily, Architects Newspaper, Bloomberg CityLab, and OPB.

“The Pickathon diversion design-build partnership offers our students a truly valuable learning experience that is rare in architectural education,” said Bell. “They participate in every step of the process, from imagination to construction — and then see it come alive in the festival environment.”

At Pickathon 2025, The Water Serpent wasn’t just a stage — it was an experience. It framed moments of music, movement, and connection in a way only Pickathon can, blending architecture, environment, and community into something magical.

b: Most festivals sell you a “General Admission” ticket to a hot, dusty field where you struggle to find shade, a seat, or a decent meal. At Pickathon the comfortable version is standard.
At Pickathon, we don’t believe you should have to buy an upgrade just to feel human. We build a Temporary City of Imagination where the “VIP” amenities are standard for every single ticket holder.
Follow the Shade: We design the schedule to keep you cool—spending days in the deep woods and nights under the stars. You’ll find curated seating everywhere.

b: A world away, 12 miles from Portland

Whether you are flying in from overseas, taking the train up the coast, embarking on a classic road trip adventure, or just commuting from your home close by, getting to Pendarvis Farm is easier than you think.

We are proud to call Happy Valley, Oregon home—located just 20 minutes from PDX Airport and 12 miles from Downtown Portland. We have designed our arrival systems to be seamless for everyone, from international travelers to local neighbors. You can immerse yourself in the fantasy for the full weekend, or come and go as you please.
For those bringing their own vehicle.
If you plan to drive, you must purchase a Weekend Parking Pass. This allows you to park in our Welcome Lot for the duration of the festival.
Welcome Lot (19208 SE Foster Rd) Note: Do not type “Pickathon” into GPS, or it will take you to the wrong gate. Use this specific address.
In-and-Out Privileges: Yes, you can leave and return as often as you like! If you are commuting daily, just flash your Parking Pass each time you return.
Carpooling: We highly encourage it! Space is limited, and it reduces our carbon footprint.
For Campers Only: The Gear Shuttle

We do not allow cars inside the festival grounds. There is one gear shuttle location for everyone arriving by vehicle (whether you drove yourself or were dropped off): the Camphost Station in the Welcome Lot. (See the Tent Camping Guide for packing rules.) Here is how you get your stuff in:

Load In (Wed–Sat): Park in the Welcome Lot and load your heavy bags onto our fleet of Gear Shuttle Trucks at the Camphost Station. You then walk a short, beautiful trail into the festival and meet your gear at the “Gear Drop” station nearest your campsite.

Load Out (Sunday, 8:00 AM – 7:00 PM / Monday, 8:00 AM – 12:00 PM): The process reverses! Haul your gear back to the Gear Drop station and place it in the zone clearly labeled TO WELCOME LOT. Then walk out to the Welcome Lot to meet your gear. Do not wait until the last minute. If you drop your gear later than 30 minutes before the service ends for the day, it may not get picked up.
Uber, Lyft, Taxi, or getting dropped off by a friend.
We have drop-off options designed to get you close to the action without needing a parking pass. Where you get dropped off depends on your gear:

If you can carry all of your gear into the festival yourself: You may be dropped off in the South Lot (the “Farmhouse Neighborhood” Main Entrance). There is no gear shuttle at the South Lot for cars/rideshare—you carry everything in on foot. South Lot / Drop-Off Zone (16581 SE Hagen Rd)

If you need the gear shuttle (because you can’t carry everything): You must be dropped off in the Welcome Lot and drop your gear at the Camphost Station (see Option 1). This is the only gear shuttle for vehicles/rideshare.
How to use the drop-off: Tell your driver to follow signs for “Pickathon Drop-Off.” Do not get out on the main road (Hagen Rd); it is unsafe.
Note: A small gear drop is available in the South Lot for bikes and ADA guests only—it is not a general gear shuttle for rideshare campers.
Thousands of attendees bike to the farm from Portland. It is a scenic ride (mostly via the Springwater Corridor).
Bike Corral: We have a secure, monitored bike parking area on-site.

Gear Haul: We offer a specialized “Bike Gear Truck” that meets guided group rides in Portland to haul your heavy camping gear to the farm for you. A small gear drop is also available in the South Lot for bikes and ADA guests.
Routes & Details: See the full Biking Guide for maps and group ride schedules.
If you want to sleep inside your vehicle (RV, Van, or Car Camping), you cannot park in the Welcome Lot. You must purchase a specific Vehicle Camping Pass (Willow or South Camp).
Entry: You will be directed to a specific gate based on your pass type.
Rules: No generators allowed. No re-entry (once your RV is parked, it stays until Monday).
Pickathon is very close to Portland International Airport (PDX).
Transit: Take the MAX Red Line from PDX Airport to “Gateway Transit Center,” transfer to the Green Line, and get off at “Lents Town Center.” From there, hop on the Pickathon Shuttle (see below).
Rideshare: An Uber/Lyft from PDX to the South Lot / Farmhouse Neighborhood Drop-Off takes approximately 25 minutes.
We run a dedicated Pickathon Shuttle connecting the Lents Town Center / Foster Rd MAX Station (Green Line) directly to the festival gates.
Shuttle Pickup (The ZED / 5716 SE 92nd Ave) Note: The shuttle does NOT stop at the train platform. You must walk to the brewery parking lot (see below).

It is easy! Walk out of Union Station to the nearby Union Station / NW 6th & Hoyt MAX stop. Hop on the Green Line (Direction: Clackamas Town Center) and ride it straight to the Lents Town Center stop.
Tickets: A Shuttle Pass must be purchased for each passenger over the age of 12.
No Parking: The shuttle stop is for MAX/Transit riders only. There is NO PARKING available at the pickup site. Do not park at The ZED / Zoiglhaus or you risk being towed.
Shuttle schedule (last year’s hours; 2027 hours post in early summer):
Frequency: Shuttles run continuous loops approx. every 45–60 minutes.
Turn Right onto SE Foster Rd.
Take a quick Right onto SE 92nd Ave.
Look for the Pickathon Shuttle Sign in front of The ZED / Zoiglhaus Brewing parking lot.
When can I arrive? These are last year’s times for planning. 2027 times post in early summer; the 2027 festival runs Wednesday, Aug 4 (early arrival) through Monday, Aug 9 (pack-out).
Note: You can leave the festival at any time, but you cannot drive in after gates close.
Everyone must be packed up and off the farm by 12:00 PM (Noon).
Drop your gear at least 30 minutes before service ends each day, or it may not get picked up. Do not wait until the last minute.
Logging Road Gear Drops — 2 Options Only:
At the Gear Drop stations along the logging road, there are only two load-out piles. Make sure your gear goes in the correct one:
Plan the rest of your trip
You know how to get here. Now make sure you are ready for the weekend.
Where to Stay — Decide between the woods (camping included!) or a nearby hotel.
Tickets & Passes Guide — Don’t forget to grab your Parking Pass or Shuttle Pass before you arrive.
Food & Drink — See what’s on the menu and learn about our reusable dishware system.

Biking to Pickathon is the cheapest and lowest climate-impact transportation option available. Plus, it’s fun! The area around Pendarvis is lovely, and you’ll get some great views on the way out here.
All attendees have the option to add on a free Bike Pass, which enables one bicycle to park inside the Pickathon grounds all weekend.

We’ll be planning a guided bike route from Reed College in Portland, where you can ride with fellow festival friends to the farm. Our bike guides will be there to help lead the way, we’ll haul all your camp gear to the festival so you don’t have to worry about a thing. After the festival ends, we’ll take all your gear back to the starting location of your bike route.

A Bicycle Pass allows one bicycle to park inside the Pickathon grounds. The Bicycle Pass is FREE, but you need to either add it to your ticket package or select it from our ticketing options to reserve room at the festival for your bicycle.

NOTE: If you’re not able to bike from Portland to Pickathon but still want to bring a bike to get from the Welcome Lot to the festival (about a mile), that’s fine. Just be sure to pick up a Bicycle Pass!

Join this curated and cultured group of bikers to pedal your way from Reed College to Pendarvis Farm via human power. Our friendly, knowledgeable biking crew will offer you a guided bike ride to the farm as well as transportation of your camping gear, allowing you to focus on enjoying your ride. Expect to ride about 11 miles on moderate hills, mostly flat urban bike paths, with access to Spring Water Corridor and some busier 2-lane roads. A good working bike, helmet, and lock are essential components to get to the farm and secure your ride.
We have a stable of bike racks at the farm to secure your bicycle once you arrive.
Maps for meet-ups and routes to Pickathon from SE Portland via Reed College
SE Ride Map from Reed College
• Thursday 7/30: Meet @ 9:30 am at SE Location (Reed College), depart location 10 am sharp. Arrive at Pickathon approx. 12 pm.
• Friday (Morning Ride) 7/31: Meet @ 9:30 am SE Location (Reed College), depart location 10:00 am sharp. Arrive at Pickathon approx. 12:00 pm.

• Friday Gear Haul: If you want to ride on your own schedule but still want all your camping gear, stop by the SE locations on Friday at 9:30 am to drop off your gear, and we will bring it to the farm for you. We have a designated 4-6 pm Gear Pick-Up on Friday by Pickathon Venue Registration. Label all your gear ahead of time with name, phone number so our bike crew can track you down to claim. Service for Bicycle Pass holders only.
Biking Back to Portland from Pendarvis Farm

Pickathon’s largest performance space. At the heart of this scenic expanse will be a series of rhythmic timber cylinders. These aren’t just supports for a stage; they are sculptures, shelters, and invitations to connect.
Deep in the heart of The Grove, something truly wild is taking root this year, and it’s growing fast. Get ready to discover “The Fractal Forest.”
The Galaxy Neighborhood returns with Gravity Pool—an immersive installation by Blackbird Public Arts that honors the movement, mythology, and magic of the festival’s Steelhead mascot.

Part woodland pub, part nostalgic hideaway — the Orchard Lounge is a cozy speakeasy tucked in the trees, featuring booth seating, classic tavern vibes, and memorabilia handpicked from 25 years of Pickathon history. Grab a drink, take a seat, and soak it all in.

Designed in partnership with AfroVillage PDX, the 2025 Windmill Neighborhood invites festival-goers into a reimagined world that celebrates the vibrant culture, philosophy, and history of the African diaspora while envisioning a future grounded in connection, sustainability, and community care.

We’ve created an entire festival within the festival just for kids and their grownups. Back for its fourth year—bigger, bolder, and more imaginative than ever. Coyote is where young festival-goers can explore music, art, and nature all weekend long.

b: Sleep under the stars or in a king-sized bed. At Pickathon, how you stay is up to you. Whether you want to wake up in the middle of the action in the deep woods or drive in from a comfortable hotel each day, we make it easy to design your perfect weekend.

The “No Comfort Tax” Philosophy: At most festivals, “General Admission Camping” means a hot, dusty field miles from the stage. At Pickathon, our standard camping is in the majestic, shaded woods of Pendarvis Farm. It is the heart of the festival, and it is included with every Weekend Ticket.

Prefer a mattress, a roof, and a private shower? Commuting to Pickathon is a pro move (and very common). We have designed the festival to be incredibly accessible for those staying off-site, visiting friends, or living in the metro area.

At Pickathon, you are camping inside a living forest. This is included with every Weekend Pass.
The Vibe: Find a spot under the Douglas Firs and settle in. The woods are naturally cool, shaded, and right next to the stages.
The Reality: This is a community experience. You will be camping on terraced trails with neighbors close by. It’s cozy, energetic, and you will leave with new friends.

b: Pickathon offers everything you need for an incredible weekend, but there are a few key things you’ll want to bring to make the most of your experience. Here’s your ultimate packing list, categorized for easy reference:
Footwear: Comfortable walking/hiking shoes are a must, as the festival grounds can get dusty.
Climate Control: Pack layers for both hot days and cool nights.
Financial Essentials: Bring a credit card or cash for vendor purchases. Your ID is also needed to pick up tickets and purchase alcohol.
Sun Protection: Pack sunscreen, a hat, and sunglasses to shield yourself from the sun.
Hydration: Bring a reusable water bottle to stay hydrated throughout the festival. Water is readily available for free on-site.
Pickathon Cup: While a stainless steel cup can be purchased at the festival, consider bringing your own with a carrying method.

Cell service is spotty in the woods; bring a battery pack, but note that public phones are unavailable. Bring your portable battery chargers or charge your devices for a fee at the solar-powered vendor.
Seating: A low-back lawn chair or blanket can provide a comfortable spot to relax and enjoy the music.
Portable Charger: Cell service might be limited, so a portable charger can keep your phone powered up (on-site charging is available for a fee).
Yoga Mat: Morning classes are available to awaken the body and refocus the mind.
Pack light as most everything you need is onsite.

Pack your camping gear in a way that allows for easy transportation to and from your campsite to the nearest Gear Drop location (which could be located within a range of 10 yards to a 1/3 of a mile up or down trails).
For more details refer to our Camping Guide.
There’s no need to pack coolers! Pickathon offers a wide variety of delicious and affordable food and drink vendors to keep you satiated all weekend.
Leave your furry friends at home: Pets are strictly prohibited.
No outside alcohol: Security checks vehicles upon entry. Outside alcohol will be confiscated.
Respectful Seating: Chairs and blankets left unattended become communal seating. Be neighborly upon your return.
Leave No Trace: Open fires, fireworks, firearms, and portable shade structures are not permitted. Camp stove usage requires extreme caution.
By packing smart and following these guidelines, you’re all set for a smooth and enjoyable Pickathon experience!
Pickathon is renowned as a pioneering leader in festival sustainability. To get there, we started with a dream.
What if Pickathon eliminated all plastic?
In 2010, Pickathon became the first major American music festival to make it happen.
Plastic beer cups were replaced with stainless steel cups that every attendee reused all weekend and took home as a collectible.
Plastic water bottles were replaced with reusable water bottles.
Water was made free and abundant.
The result of eliminating plastic was our waste volume went down by over 40%.
We were excited but not 100% satisfied, as we knew the huge volume of compostable dishware at most music festivals ends up in the landfill. This inspired a new dream!
What if Pickathon eliminated all single-use dishware/utensils?
In 2011, Pickathon became the first major American music festival to eliminate all single-use food dishes & utensils, replacing them with reusable bamboo-based dishes + utensils that we wash on-site.
Eliminating single use dishware reduced our waste by an additional 30%.
Covid shut the festival down for two years, but during this time, a new dream was born.
What if we minimized our carbon footprint by using time and natural terrain?
In 2022, Pickathon redesigned the entire festival experience to better fit within the environmental footprint of Pendarvis Farm.
During the day when the sun is burning hot, performances take place in thickly wooded locations to provide a cool shaded experience to the performers and audience.
As the sun goes down and the crowds swell, we move to huge open meadows to finish the day under the stars.
This made Pickathon’s festival experience better in every way, and led to us enshrining one of our three core design principles – Nature is the Best Vibe.
Here’s what else we do every year to keep Pickathon environmentally sustainable:Recycling & Compost
Pickathon’s recycling and compost team is made up of volunteers who spend most of the festival rounding up everything that can be either recycled or composted.

Pendarvis Farm hosts a permanent solar array on the roof of the Galaxy Barn. The energy generated during the year offsets 100% of the energy used during the festival in the Galaxy Barn plus a portion of the electricity used by the food and craft vendors.
Pickathon financially incentivizes our audience to ride bikes and take mass transportation to Pickathon to minimize the total carbon footprint of Pickathon.

community.t: Creative Neighborhoods: we build things for you
b: Creative Neighborhoods, our nonprofit design-build partner, is the team behind Pickathon’s neighborhoods. Every stage, bar, patio and gathering place you see on the farm is designed with leading architects and builders, stands at Pickathon for one weekend, and then goes to work somewhere else for years.
If you need a stage, a patio, a pavilion, a classroom or a play space, we can design it with you and build it. It debuts at Pickathon in front of thousands of people, then we deliver it to your site.
Businesses and private owners: you bring the budget. We aim to come in at least 10% under the open-market price, with a structure designed by top architects.
Nonprofits and community groups with a budget: it works the same way.
Nonprofits still raising money: we can help you find partners to fund the build.

Recent builds went to Parrott Creek Child & Family Services (outdoor classrooms), Sabin CDC (gardens and gathering spaces at 17 properties), Dream Plaza 2.0 in Portland’s Central Eastside, Girls Build, and Alliance Charter Academy.
We push what a building can be

The festival is a testing ground. Each year our design teams try new structures, materials and ways of putting a building together and taking it apart, so it can be reused instead of thrown away. That work has earned AIA design awards.
Students and apprentices build alongside working architects and carpenters, from Portland State architecture students to youth shop programs. They leave with real projects and real skills.

Pickathon has built its neighborhoods by hand for two decades. In 2023 we started Creative Neighborhoods to keep that mission work alive, and launched it in 2024 so the building work could stand on its own and serve the community year-round.
Ready to talk about a project? Use the Build with Pickathon form, or email info@pickathon.com.

You think you know music festivals? Pickathon will make you rethink everything. Leave your expectations at the gate. This isn’t your typical festival, it’s a portal to a different world of music. Imagine stumbling upon your new favorite band while wandering through a sun-dappled forest.

We don’t just book headliners; we cultivate a community of groundbreaking artists. You’ll leave with a playlist full of hidden gems and stories of ‘I saw them before they were big.’ The smaller size of the fest and the multiple performances give you a much higher chance of actually meeting some of the artists.

Imagine stages nestled among towering trees, where the music blends seamlessly with the sounds of nature. Feel the cool forest air, hear the music resonate through the trees, and taste the locally sourced flavors – Pickathon is a feast for the senses. This isn’t just a backdrop; it’s an integral part of the experience, providing shade and comfort.

More than just a festival, Pickathon is a gathering of like-minded souls. We prioritize sustainability with our reusable dish program and creating a space where you can connect with nature and each other guilt-free. Enjoy the significant savings that come with free camping.

Pickathon has a reputation for being something special, an experience that those who’ve been understand on a deeper level. Join the ‘IYKYK’ (if you know, you know) crowd and discover why. Pickathon is a “word of mouth” festival. Once you experience the magic, you’ll never look at festivals the same way again.
Follow us on Instagram at @pickathon for real-time updates and more!

There’s a common saying among those who return to Pendarvis Farm year after year: “You won’t understand unless you come.” It’s an understatement. How do you describe a place that feels less like a music festival and more like a summer camp for the soul? It’s a world built for wandering, for connection, and for the kind of joyous discovery that sticks with you long after the weekend is over.

The secret is that Pickathon is an experience where everything is intertwined. The world-class music, the stunning architecture, and the beautiful natural landscape don’t just coexist—they enrich each other to create something truly different.

We don’t just set up stages in a field; we build a temporary city within a lush, 80-acre forest. Winding paths lead you through groves of trees to a series of distinct “neighborhoods.” To see how it all connects, you can view the festival map and learn more in our guide to Getting Around Pickathon.
Each neighborhood is a functional work of art, featuring large-scale, ephemeral structures created by world-class architects and designers.
These aren’t just decorations; they are the stages, bars, and gathering spots, all built in harmony with the natural surroundings. This is the stunning world you get to live in for four days.

This unique environment is the driving force behind everything else. It’s what makes the discovery of music here so profound. We are a legendary launching pad for future icons, and our stages are designed to be the most memorable settings to see them for the first time. The universe of artists who played here just before they broke out is vast, including a select few like Sturgill Simpson, Billy Strings, Tyler Childers, Future Islands, Lake Street Dive, Shakey Graves, Khruangbin, and Black Pumas.

This design also creates a feeling of freedom. With most artists playing twice, the frantic pressure of other festivals disappears. You have the time to follow your curiosity, stumble upon a mind-blowing meal from an award-winning chef, or relax in a hidden oasis. The experience is yours to create.

It all rests on a foundation of respect for the land and for each other. Our commitment to sustainability and community is what fosters the famously relaxed, safe, and friendly atmosphere that makes this “summer camp for the soul” possible. It’s a world built to be explored, and we invite you to come, get lost, and find something new.

press.q: Pickathon showed why it’s the best indie festival in the country.
…where the best artists look as if they’d been whittled from the surrounding woods.
Imagine a music festival without any of the worst parts of a music festival.
Play Pickathon well, the story goes, and you just might make it big.
Pickathon has become known for getting an early jump on acts about to break big.
Welcome to Pickathon, perhaps America’s most unique and highly-curated music festival.
Pickathon doesn’t attract the same kind of attention as its peers — and that’s by design.
It remains the best festival I’ve ever been to, by a fairly wide margin, and I’ve been to a bunch.
With a zero-waste ethos, the Pickathon festival combines art, architecture, food and music.
The greenest festival in North America.

chapters.h: It started as a benefit with 200 people
x: In 1999, a volunteer crew threw a benefit for KBOO community radio at Horning’s Hideout: roots musicians on a hand-built wooden stage by a lake, in front of about 200 people.

In 2005 we lost that home and landed in a hayfield called Pudding River. There was no shade, so the crowd built it: sewer poles and shade cloth bought off a train car. The audience became the crew, and it has been that way since.
In 2006 we moved to Pendarvis Farm in Happy Valley, 12 miles from Portland. We have been here ever since.

chapters.h: The farm is where the discovery started
x: Our first year on the farm, the Avett Brothers played the Galaxy Barn before most people knew them. That set the pattern: book artists on the way up, and give them a room worth remembering.
Billy Strings, Leon Bridges, Tyler Childers, Big Thief, Khruangbin, The Marías, Wet Leg and Geese all played here early. At least 44 alumni got their first Grammy nomination after playing the farm.
Next to the new names, we bring back the artists who built the music: Mavis Staples, Tinariwen, Yo La Tengo, King Sunny Adé, Phil Lesh, Taj Mahal, Steve Earle, Marcos Valle and many more.
The one that got away: the 2020 lineup, canceled by the pandemic, had John Prine, Sierra Ferrell, (Sandy) Alex G and Joan Shelley.

chapters.h: We filmed it so you could see it
x: For years, a film crew of hundreds captured sets across the farm: more than 1,100 videos on our YouTube channel, from Mandolin Orange’s “Wake Me” to Tyler Childers in the On the Farm Sessions.
“We have no boxes, no normal stages. We design every space as a sculpture or a theme park for music fans.” That was 2013, and it still holds. The Woods Stage is carved into the trees.

The Treeline Stage was designed and built with Portland State University architecture students. It won an AIA Portland Architecture Award in 2015, a Citation Award in 2017, and Gray Magazine’s first Design for Good award, after the 2017 stage became sleeping pods for veterans in Clackamas County.

Since 2022 the whole farm has been split into neighborhoods, each designed and built by its own team. After the festival, the structures go on to permanent homes: a skatepark, a school, a garden greenhouse.

chapters.h: No single-use plates or cups, for years
x: In 2010 we banned single-use plastic cups. Now every plate and cup on the farm is reusable, and water is free. Billboard put it this way in 2014: “an annual festival whose 3,500 attendees contribute almost nothing to area landfills.”

Lumber from the neighborhoods is reused and donated instead of hauled away. Since 2024, our nonprofit design-build partner Creative Neighborhoods has led the work and found each structure its next home.
